title: Table songs
tomorrow: the Torah never mentions phones. so why do some put them away?

lines: THE BOWLS ARE EMPTY. NOBODY GETS UP.
cards: Friday night, Noa's kitchen. The soup bowls are empty, the challah is down to crumbs, and nobody gets up. Saba David taps the table twice with a spoon and starts to hum.
No words at first, just yai-dai-dai, low and slow. On the second round, Owen's grandfather finds a harmony underneath it. Noa, who swore she couldn't sing, drums on the table.
By the third round the whole table is going, and nobody announced a song or handed out lyrics. So what just happened here, and why is it so much older than anyone at this table?

teach.b: What happened is zemirot: table songs, sung at Shabbat meals, between courses or before the blessing after eating. The word means songs, and a Psalm uses it: "Thy statutes have been my songs."
The idea runs back to the Temple.

teach.h: A PSALM FOR THE SABBATH DAY.
teach.b: The Mishnah lists a psalm the Levites sang there for each day of the week, and for Shabbat it was the one titled "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day."

teach.h: THE TABLE IN PLACE OF THE ALTAR.
teach.b: Then the Temple was gone, and the Talmud says something startling: once the altar atoned for Israel; now a person's table does. If the table stands in for the altar, it gets the altar's music too.
So the songs moved from the Temple courts to the kitchen. Over the centuries poets kept writing new ones, in Hebrew and Aramaic.
One table favorite, Yah Ribon, by the poet Israel Najara, opens in Aramaic: God, master of the world and of all worlds.
Some tables sing a niggun instead, a tune with no words at all, which is exactly what Saba was doing. That's the part to tell a friend tonight: you don't need to know the words to join. A hum counts.
Zemirot aren't a test you can fail; they're closer to a family singing at a birthday, except this birthday comes every week. The point isn't a performance.
It's a table that doesn't want the meal to end.

how: At Shabbat dinner and lunch, families sing zemirot between courses or before the blessing after the meal, from small songbooks or by heart; some tables sing wordless tunes, called niggunim.

songs sung around the table at Shabbat meals

games.q: your friend says her family's Friday dinners go quiet and awkward once the food is gone. she asks what a Shabbat table does with that lull. what fits?
o: sing: table songs fill the time between the food and the blessing after.
put on a playlist of Jewish music so the room isn't silent.
clear the plates fast; the meal is over once the food is.
games.why: zemirot live exactly there, after the courses and before the blessing after eating. a playlist is music; a table song is the table itself joining in.

practice: Pick one tune you can carry: a Shabbat song you know, a melody from your own family, or just yai-dai-dai. Hum it once softly, then once a little louder, tapping the beat on a table or your knee.
If no tune comes, hum one low note on each out-breath and let that be your song.

wordCard.voice: Zemirot: table songs. Sung at Shabbat meals, from the Temple's psalm to a wordless hum over the crumbs.

orig.note: Hebrew: songs. the same word appears in Psalm 119:54, "thy statutes have been my songs."

carryVoice: Pocket this one: sing at the table, even if a hum is all you've got. See you tomorrow.
